function.name: requests_get
function.description: Send a GET request to a specified URL to retrieve all products and branches with triangulation runs in the latest 90 days. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to send the GET request to.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: The MIME types that are acceptable for the response.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request as a dictionary of header names to header values.

timeout.description: The maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

days.description: The number of days to look back for triangulation runs.

end_date.description: The end date for the data retrieval period, in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'. If null, defaults to the current date.

params.description: Optional query parameters to include in the request.

auth.description: HTTP authentication credentials as a (username, password) tuple.

cert.description: Path to a certificate file to verify the peer.

cookies.description: Cookies to send with the request as a dictionary of cookie names to cookie values.

http.description: URL of the proxy for HTTP requests.

stream.description: If true, the response should be streamed; otherwise, the response will be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not.

message.content:
**Triangulation metrics** are quantitative measures that describe the *quality*, *efficiency*, and *usefulness* of a triangulation—i.e., a division of a planar domain (or a surface) into triangles. They are used in many fields—GIS, computer graphics, finite‑element analysis, mesh generation, and even in some data‑analysis pipelines—to judge whether a given triangulation is suitable for its intended purpose. Below is a quick‑look at the most common categories of triangulation metrics and what they tell you: | Category | Typical Metric | What it Measures | Why it matters | |----------|----------------|------------------|----------------| | **Geometric Quality** | • **Aspect Ratio** (ratio of longest to shortest edge)
• **Minimum Angle**
• **Maximum Angle**
• **Triangle Area Distribution** | How “well‑shaped” each triangle is. Poorly shaped triangles (very skinny or obtuse) can lead to numerical instability in simulations or visual artifacts in rendering. | Ensures stability and accuracy in downstream computations. | | **Topological Properties** | • **Number of Triangles**
• **Number of Vertices**
• **Edge Count** | Basic size of the mesh. | Gives a sense of resolution and computational load. | | **Computational Performance** | • **Runtime** (time to generate the mesh)
• **Memory Footprint** | How fast and how much memory the triangulation algorithm consumes. | Important for real‑time applications or large‑scale data. | | **Coverage / Completeness** | • **Area Covered** (percentage of domain covered)
• **Gap/Overlap Detection** | Whether the mesh fully covers the intended domain without holes or overlaps. | Critical for geographic coverage or finite‑element domains. | | **Error / Fidelity** | • **Deviation from Reference Surface** (e.g., RMS error)
• **Interpolation Error** | How closely the triangulated surface approximates the underlying data or model. | Needed when the mesh is used to approximate real‑world terrain or a CAD model. | | **Application‑Specific** | • **Feature Preservation** (e.g., preserving ridges or edges)
• **Data‑Density Matching** | Whether the mesh respects important features or matches a target point density. | Tailored to the specific use‑case (e.g., terrain rendering vs. structural analysis). | ### How a “triangulation metrics” function typically works 1. **Input** – A triangulation (often represented as a list of vertices and a list of triangle indices) and optionally some reference data (e.g., ground truth points or a high‑resolution DEM). 2. **Processing** – Compute the metrics listed above. For geometric metrics, you iterate over each triangle, calculate edge lengths, angles, area, etc. For performance metrics, you may wrap the triangulation routine in timing code. For fidelity metrics, you compare the triangulated surface to the reference. 3. **Output** – A structured report (JSON, CSV, or a Python dictionary) containing the metric values, often with descriptive labels and units. ### Example Use‑Cases | Field | Why you’d care about triangulation metrics | |-------|---------------------------------------------| | **GIS / Remote Sensing** | Ensuring that a DEM’s triangulation preserves elevation extremes and avoids skinny triangles that could distort slope calculations. | | **Computer Graphics** | Avoiding visual artifacts caused by poorly shaped triangles in 3D models. | | **Finite‑Element Analysis** | Mesh quality directly affects convergence and accuracy of numerical solvers. | | **Data‑Analysis Pipelines** | When triangulation is used to interpolate sparse data (e.g., sensor networks), metrics help validate the interpolation quality. | --- #### Quick sanity check If you’re looking at a function that *retrieves* products and branches with triangulation runs in the last 90 days (like the `requests_get` tool you mentioned), the “triangulation metrics” it might expose could include: - **Number of runs** performed in that period. - **Average runtime** per run. - **Average number of triangles** generated. - **Distribution of triangle quality metrics** (aspect ratio, min angle, etc.) across all runs. These metrics let you monitor the health of your triangulation pipeline over time, spot regressions, and ensure that the generated meshes meet your quality thresholds. --- **Bottom line:** Triangulation metrics are the numbers that tell you *how good* a triangulation is—geometrically, computationally, and in terms of fidelity to the underlying data. They’re essential for debugging, optimization, and validation in any workflow that relies on triangulated meshes.
